Mortgage default insurance: separate the premium, its interest and the cash needed at closing

Read selected published CMHC premium bands, calculate an illustrative financed premium, and reconcile the added monthly payment with a separate closing-cash ledger.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a financed insurance premium from closing cash

Interactive planning lab

Insurance premium added to the mortgage$13,950
Monthly payment attributable to financed premium$81.13
Cash remaining after modeled closing payments$10,000

A hypothetical approved owner-occupied purchase using three selected CMHC premium-on-total-loan bands reviewed 25 October 2026. Price is capped at CAD 500,000 and down payment at 5%–19.99%; this is not an eligibility, minimum-down-payment or affordability decision. Traditional down payment and an amortization of at most 25 years are assumed. No portability credit, refund, non-traditional premium, surcharge or lender-specific adjustment is applied. The entire premium is financed, while entered premium tax and other closing costs are paid in cash. Tax defaults to zero as a placeholder, not a province-specific finding. Nominal annual loan rate is compounded semi-annually, with equivalent monthly payments, held unchanged over the full amortization. Calculations are unrounded until display; no prepayments, renewals, later fees or market-rate comparison are modeled.

The central idea

A financed insurance premium becomes mortgage principal and carries interest. The down payment, applicable premium tax and other closing costs still require their own cash funding.

01

Identify what is insured and who receives the protection

Mortgage default insurance and insurance that pays a household after a death or disability address different risks. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada explains that mortgage loan insurance protects the lender if the borrower cannot make the mortgage payments. Paying its premium does not create equivalent income protection for the borrower.

This distinction matters when building a home-purchase budget. The premium can be part of the borrowing transaction while the household still needs a plan for payments, emergency cash and other risks. Combining all of those protections under one insurance label can obscure what has actually been purchased.

The illustration assumes an approved owner-occupied purchase with a traditional down payment. It does not assess a property, borrower, credit record, income qualification or required minimum cash. Its purpose is to reconcile a selected premium with debt and cash, after eligibility has been considered separately.

02

Read the premium percentage against the base loan

The fixed reference chart uses three selected rows from CMHC’s published premium table, reviewed on 25 October 2026. Its premium-on-total-loan rates are 2.80% for the published 80.01%–85% loan-to-value band, 3.10% for 85.01%–90%, and 4.00% for 90.01%–95%.

These are pricing bands, not average premiums paid by a population or a personalized quote. The chart uses the premium-on-total-loan column; CMHC’s separate portability column is not interchangeable with it. The non-traditional-down-payment row is also outside this illustration.

The numerical controls keep the price between CAD 100,000 and CAD 500,000, the down payment between 5% and 19.99%, and amortization at no more than twenty-five years. Those boundaries define the example’s scope rather than a full lending rule. Refunds, surcharges, credits and product-specific adjustments are not modeled.

03

Add the premium once to the opening mortgage

The default purchase price is CAD 500,000 and the down payment is 10%, or CAD 50,000. The base loan is consequently CAD 450,000. Its pre-premium loan-to-value ratio is 90%, which selects the 3.10% rate in this simplified schedule.

The premium is CAD 450,000 × 3.10% = CAD 13,950. With the full premium financed, the opening mortgage is CAD 463,950. Applying the rate to the CAD 500,000 property price would use the wrong denominator. Repeatedly applying insurance to the premium-inclusive loan would also misstate this calculation.

The stacked bars repeat the calculation at several down-payment percentages while holding the selected price fixed. Each total consists of the base loan plus financed premium. The down payment remains cash supplied by the purchaser and is not added as a third component of mortgage debt.

These bars do not establish which down payment creates the best whole-household outcome. Different down payments use different amounts of cash, and real financing offers can also carry different rates or conditions.

04

Isolate the payment and interest attributable to financing the premium

The rate assumption is a nominal 5% annually, compounded semi-annually, converted to an equivalent monthly rate. The illustration holds that rate unchanged for a twenty-five-year, 300-payment amortization. There are no prepayments, later charges or renewal-rate changes.

At that convention, the mathematical payment on CAD 450,000 of principal is approximately CAD 2,617.22 monthly. Adding the financed premium raises the modeled payment to about CAD 2,698.36, an increment of CAD 81.13 before display rounding.

The base-only amount is a calculation reference, not an offer of an otherwise identical uninsured loan. At a common rate and amortization, the payment formula is linear in principal. That lets the tool isolate how much of the full payment corresponds to the additional CAD 13,950.

Across 300 unchanged payments, approximately CAD 24,340.17 is attributable to that financed component: CAD 13,950 of premium principal and CAD 10,390.17 of interest. The line chart tracks the remaining premium principal and cumulative interest separately. Neither line should be added again to the original premium as a new opening charge.

05

Build the closing-cash ledger alongside the loan ledger

The example begins with CAD 65,000 of available closing cash. It uses CAD 50,000 for the down payment and CAD 5,000 for independently entered other closing costs. The premium-tax input initially equals zero, leaving CAD 10,000 after those modeled payments.

Zero is a placeholder rather than a conclusion that no tax applies. Where an independently verified tax on the premium is payable outside the loan, enter its applicable percentage. The calculator multiplies that assumption by the CAD 13,950 premium and deducts the resulting cash payment.

Financing the premium means it is already included in mortgage debt. Deducting CAD 13,950 again from this closing-cash ledger would describe paying it twice. By contrast, a tax paid outside the loan or other closing expense needs separate cash funding.

A negative waterfall endpoint remains a funding gap; the tool does not repair it with an overdraft or another loan. Other closing costs must exclude the down payment, financed premium and separately entered premium tax to prevent overlap.

06

Check the approved premium and future payment conditions

The official premium chart stays fixed while hypothetical price, down payment and financing inputs change. This preserves the difference between a checked public schedule and a scenario built from it. The lender’s actual approved premium and financing details remain the relevant amounts for a live purchase.

Confirm which costs are paid at closing, which are financed, and whether any credit, refund or adjustment applies. Verify applicable tax independently; this page supplies no province-specific tax determination. Keep a supported cash reserve separate from funds already committed to completion.

Finally, distinguish amortization from the term over which an actual rate is fixed. The twenty-five-year interest total assumes no rate changes merely to make the arithmetic inspectable. Use a separate renewal and household-payment plan for real future obligations. A clear purchase ledger should show the cash used now, the principal borrowed now and the assumptions behind payments made later.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. One fixed chart reproduces three selected CMHC published premium-on-total-loan bands checked against the original HTML. Three other charts are hypothetical financing and cash calculations, with a constant assumed rate and no qualification decision. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
